title: ServSafe Manager Certified: Your Person-in-Charge Duties
description: Why food jobs ask for a certified food protection manager, how an inspector checks you, the duties the FDA Food Code lists, and what the 2026 edition adds.
intro: Passing the ServSafe Food Protection Manager exam makes you a certified food protection manager (often shortened to CFPM). The certificate matters at work because of one model rulebook: the FDA Food Code. It says who must hold this certificate, how a health inspector checks the person in charge, and which daily duties that person is responsible for. This guide explains those rules in plain words, shows what the newest edition (the 2026 Food Code) adds, and tells you how to find the rules that actually apply where you work.

sections.heading: Why a food job asks for this certificate
sections.body:
Section 2-102.12 of the FDA Food Code says the **person in charge** (PIC) of a food establishment shall be a certified food protection manager who passed a test that is part of an accredited program. Section 2-101.11 says a person in charge must be present during all hours of operation. Put together, the model code expects a certified manager to be the one running each shift.

There is one built-in exception: the rule does not apply to establishments that the regulatory authority (your state or local health department) decides pose minimal risk of foodborne illness, based on the kind of operation and how much food is prepared.

Not every certificate counts. Under section 2-102.20, a certificate meets the rule when the certification program is evaluated and listed by an accrediting agency recognized by the Conference for Food Protection (CFP). The Food Code's background notes (Annex 3) explain that the ANSI National Accreditation Board (ANAB) does this evaluation under an agreement with the CFP.

sections.heading: The Food Code is a model, so your local rules decide
sections.body:
The FDA writes the Food Code, but it is a model. FDA says restaurant and retail food store oversight is usually handled at the state and local level, and states adopt the code on their own schedule, sometimes with changes.

FDA's 2024 adoption report shows how uneven this is. As of 2024, 11 state agencies in 7 states had adopted the 2022 edition (then the newest). 30 state agencies in 24 states had adopted either the 2022 or the 2017 edition. So the edition your inspector uses may be several years older than the newest one.

Annex 3 also leaves certain choices to state and local agencies: which types of establishments can be exempt from the manager certification rule, and when a place must have more than one certified manager. The factors it lists include the size of the operation, hours of operation, the types of food, how much food is prepared on site, the number of staff, whether the people served are highly susceptible (for example, nursing home residents), and the number of meals served. That is why two restaurants in different counties can have different staffing rules.

sections.heading: How an inspector checks the person in charge
sections.body:
The inspection report guide in Annex 7 of the Food Code has two separate items for the person in charge.

**Item 1: present, shows knowledge, performs duties.** The PIC can show knowledge in any one of three ways (section 2-102.11):

1. Being a certified food protection manager from an accredited program.
2. Having no violations of priority items during the current inspection. (Priority items are rules that directly control a hazard, such as cooking, cooling, reheating, and handwashing.)
3. Answering the inspector's questions correctly for that operation. The code lists the topics, from employee hygiene and cooking temperatures to cleaning and sanitizing, water supply, chemicals, and major food allergens.

**Item 2: certified food protection manager.** This item is marked in compliance when the PIC is a certified food protection manager, and out of compliance when no PIC is certified or the certificate is not from an accredited program.

So a good answer to the inspector's questions can satisfy Item 1, but in a jurisdiction that follows section 2-102.12, it does not replace the certificate for Item 2. Keep your certificate where you can show it during an inspection.

sections.heading: The daily duties the code puts on you
sections.body:
Section 2-103.11 says the person in charge maintains **active managerial control** of foodborne illness risk factors. Annex 3 describes this as having systems in place, checked through talking with the PIC and seeing that the systems actually work. The listed duties include making sure that:

- People who are not needed stay out of food prep, storage, and dishwashing areas, and visitors such as delivery and pest control workers follow the code.
- Employees wash their hands well, with the PIC routinely watching.
- Deliveries are checked on arrival for approved source, temperature, and condition, including deliveries left during non-operating hours.
- Cooking temperatures are checked with properly scaled and calibrated thermometers, and cooling, hot and cold holding, and thawing temperatures are monitored, with daily oversight by the PIC.
- Customers who order raw or undercooked animal foods are informed (the consumer advisory).
- Sanitizing is checked: water temperature and time for hot water, and concentration, pH, temperature, and time for chemicals.
- Ready-to-eat food is not touched with bare hands unless the health department has approved an alternative.
- Employees are trained for their duties, including food allergy awareness, and are told in a way that can be verified that they must report certain illnesses.

The annex says this inspection item is marked out of compliance for a pattern of failures, not for one isolated slip. These duties line up with the ServSafe exam. ServSafe's blueprint gives 15 of the 80 scored questions to preparation and cooking and 13 to receiving, storage, transportation, and disposal, so what you studied for those areas is what you will be supervising.

sections.heading: What the 2026 Food Code adds for managers
sections.body:
FDA released the 2026 Food Code, and its Summary of Changes lists several items that affect the person in charge:

- **Food defense knowledge.** A new knowledge area, 2-102.11(C)(18), covers the steps taken to prevent people from deliberately contaminating food, such as watching operations, ingredients, and supplies for unusual or suspicious activity.
- **Food defense awareness for staff.** New paragraph 2-103.11(R) says the person in charge makes sure employees are aware of signs of deliberate tampering as it relates to their jobs and report suspicious activity to the person in charge.
- **Active managerial control in the rule itself.** The opening sentence of 2-103.11 now states that the PIC maintains active managerial control by ensuring the listed duties are met.
- **A written employee illness policy.** New section 2-501.11 requires the permit holder to have a written employee illness policy, available on request. It must cover reporting of the symptoms of diarrhea, vomiting, sore throat with fever, jaundice, or infected wounds or cuts; diagnoses of norovirus, hepatitis A, Shigella, typhoid fever, non-typhoidal Salmonella, or Shiga toxin-producing E. coli; and when a worker is excluded or restricted and when they can return. The written clean-up procedure for vomiting and diarrhea events moved to section 2-502.11.

These apply to you only after your state or local health department adopts the 2026 edition. The practice questions on this site follow the 2022 Food Code numbers.

sections.heading: Keeping the certificate valid when you move
sections.body:
ServSafe says the National Restaurant Association recognizes the ServSafe Food Protection Manager Certification for five years, but state or employer requirements can differ. Check your health department's rule before you assume five years.

Moving to another state or county is where accreditation helps. In a letter reprinted in Annex 3, FDA encourages agencies at every level of government to accept certificates from certifiers listed under the ANAB-CFP accreditation program, so managers do not have to repeat training and testing when they cross jurisdiction lines. That is encouragement, not a guarantee. Each jurisdiction still makes its own rule, so confirm before you start a new job.

sections.heading: What to do this week
sections.body:
1. Find your state on FDA's "State Retail and Food Service Codes and Regulations by State" page and open your state's food code.
2. In that code, look for the person in charge and food protection manager sections. Note which Food Code edition it is based on, whether it requires a certified manager on every shift, and how long a certificate stays valid there.
3. Ask your employer whether the establishment has a written employee illness policy and a written vomit and diarrhea clean-up procedure, and read both.
4. Put your certificate, or a copy, where you can reach it during an inspection.
5. Write down your certificate's issue date and set a reminder well before it expires.
6. If you have not passed yet, finish the preparation and cooking and the receiving and storage chapters first, since they carry the most questions.

faq.question: Does every cook need the ServSafe Manager certificate?
faq.answer: Not under the FDA Food Code. Section 2-102.12 puts the requirement on the person in charge. Other staff are covered by training duties under 2-103.11, and some places have their own food handler card rules, so check your local health department.

faq.question: Can I pass an inspection without a certificate if I answer every question?
faq.answer: Correct answers can meet the knowledge part of the inspection (section 2-102.11). The inspection guide checks the certified manager rule as a separate item, so where section 2-102.12 is adopted, the person in charge still needs a certificate from an accredited program unless the establishment is exempt as minimal risk.

faq.question: Is the 2026 Food Code already the law in my state?
faq.answer: Only if your state or local agency has adopted it. FDA's 2024 report showed that only 11 state agencies in 7 states had adopted the 2022 edition at that time. Your state's food code page will show which edition it follows.
